intelligence.essence: The director merges with his own hand. When the queue backs up, he sweeps it himself — he has cleared hundreds of parked changes this way. But his click is trust, not review: he cannot see the code, so when he merges, he is counting on the seat who put the work forward to have already done the job right. A change left sitting merge-ready without its scorecard has quietly handed its review to a man who cannot perform it. That is the director's law, spoken 2026-10-26: scorecard it first, then merge it yourself — the breach was never his click; the breach is the unscored work sitting in his path.
intelligence.human_view:
Every team runs on trust, and trust is healthiest when nobody has to spend it blindly. When work piles up, the director clears it himself, clicking through hundreds of changes the team left parked. Each click says: I trust the person who put this here checked it properly. He cannot open the code and check it himself — that was never his job. His job is direction. The checking belongs to the seat that did the work.

So the honest way to honor that trust is simple: never hand him work that isn't already proven. Do the review yourself, write the score down where everyone can see it, and once it is solid, land it yourself. Then his trust is never spent on a gamble — it is spent on a certainty the team already earned. And when something does slip through that shouldn't have, the failure belongs to whoever proposed it, not to the trust that carried it.

The evidence, so this is not abstract: over recent days the director cleared a backlog of roughly six hundred parked changes down to under ten, by hand. On 2026-10-26 at 03:01–03:03Z, six changes merged inside 74 seconds with zero reviews and no scorecards on record. Their substance was afterwards verified byte-for-byte — the documents landed exactly as written — but the form failed completely, and the record at first blamed the shared login instead of the seats who had parked the work unscored. The director corrected the accounting himself the same hour.
intelligence.simple_view:
Imagine you finish your drawing and you want the teacher to hang it on the wall. Before you hand it in, you check it yourself: did I color inside the lines? Did I write my name? Is it really finished?

You don't just hand the teacher a drawing you never looked at and hope she checks it for you — because when she hangs it up, she's trusting that YOU already checked. Checking is your job. Handing it in is hers.

And if your drawing has a big scribble you never noticed because you never looked — that's not the teacher's fault for hanging it. It's yours, for not looking. Check it first. Then hand it in proud.
intelligence.grandma_view: It's about not taking advantage of someone's trust, dear. When work piles up, Shawn goes through it himself and says yes, yes, yes — hundreds of times — because he trusts his team did things properly. He can't look inside every piece of work; that's not what a director does. So the kind and honest thing is: nobody gives him work that hasn't been checked first. You check your own work, you write down that you checked it, and then you finish it yourself. That way his trust is never wasted on something nobody bothered to look at. And if something wrong slips through, we don't blame the man who trusted us. We look at who handed it to him unchecked. That's just fair.
intelligence.naya_view:
Purpose: the merge doctrine for every seat. The architectural rule — the law, in plain words:

1. Never put a change forward that is not right. Scorecard it before it enters the queue in a mergeable state — the scorecard is the review, and it happens first, every time.
2. If a merge is good, there is no problem. If a change goes through that should not have, the failure belongs to the seat that proposed it — not to the director who carried it on trust.
3. Once the work is scorecarded and solid, the seat merges it itself. Agents land their own proven work; the queue never waits for the director to sweep it clear.
4. Parking work "on hold for scorecard" in the director's path is the defect in a polite costume: it feeds unscored work to his sweep. Complete the scorecard, then land it — or do not leave it merge-ready. Staged work that must wait opens as a DRAFT (L679) so it cannot be swept.
5. His click authorizes nothing and proves nothing. Substance is proven by the scorecard and by the bytes, exactly as before.

The test: before you open a change, ask — is its scorecard already done, by a different seat, at its exact head? If not, it does not go in merge-ready. After it lands, ask — did we land it ourselves, on the strength of that scorecard? If the director's hand moved it, we left him our job: note it, and do not repeat it.
intelligence.ai_view:
SN-0336 already taught the merging seat's own discipline — score it, deconflict it, then merge — and SN-0781 taught that the scorecard must run the gate. This note adds what those did not carry: the director himself is the queue's sweeper of last resort, his merge is an act of trust rather than a review, and the duty therefore sits upstream — no seat may leave unscored work where his trust will carry it through.

Scorecard it first. Then merge it yourself. Never make the director's trust do the review.

— Naya Resolve, for Team Naya, at the director's word, 2026-10-26 (full-form upgrade the same day: a note about doing the whole job should be the whole note)
